text: That night: as he speaks, Holmes draws the dog-whip from the dead man's lap
why: ¶246 says Holmes drew the dog-whip swiftly from the dead man's lap as he spoke; the night setting is established throughout.

text: That night: Holmes throws the noose round the reptile's neck
why: ¶246 states he threw the noose round the reptile's neck.

text: That night: Holmes throws the reptile into the iron safe
why: ¶246 states he threw the snake into the iron safe.

text: That night: Holmes closes the safe upon the reptile
why: ¶246 states he closed the safe upon it.

text: How was the snake got from the safe to the bed and back?
why: The snake was in Roylott's room and then in the safe, and the story has shown a route via the ventilator and bell-pull, so the question of how it moved between the safe and the bed is a fair one for the reader to ask.

text: How was the snake got from the safe to the bed and back? — it was trained to come back to the whistle, for the milk
id: q.how_snake_worked=it was trained to come back to the whistle, for the milk
why: The whistle, the saucer of milk on the safe (¶165), and Holmes lashing at the bell-pull at the whistle give the reader reason to consider a trained snake coming back to a whistle for milk.

text: How was the snake got from the safe to the bed and back? — he put it up to the ventilator by hand, with the noose on the lash
id: q.how_snake_worked=he put it up to the ventilator by hand, with the noose on the lash
why: The loop of whipcord on the bed (¶169) and the snake being on Roylott's head make a hand-carried route a possibility the reader has reason to consider.

text: How was the snake got from the safe to the bed and back? — it was left to find its own way down the rope
id: q.how_snake_worked=it was left to find its own way down the rope
why: The bell-rope hangs from a hook above the ventilator (¶151), so a snake descending the rope is a possibility the story gives reason to consider.

text: What made the clanging sound? — the snake's den is the iron safe, and its door shuts on it
why: The story has not said the clang Helen heard on Julia's night was the safe door; that is a new causal claim about the earlier night. The safe-as-den detail appears only in ¶245-246, and the story's own proposed explanation for the clang is the metal bars (¶90).

text: What is the small dog lash tied into a loop for? — with the noose a snake can be caught by the neck and carried at arm's length
why: ¶246 shows Holmes using the noose on the whip to catch the snake by the neck and carry it at arm's length.
